analysis.one_liner: Ends the special exemption that lets freight railroads set rates and merge free of antitrust law.
analysis.headline: The Railroad Antitrust Enforcement Act cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on December 19, 2007 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Freight railroads have long been exempt from the antitrust laws that apply to almost every other industry. They can agree among themselves on shipping rates and win merger approvals that cannot be challenged in court, and customers suing over anticompetitive conduct cannot recover triple damages. This bill would strip those exemptions: railroads would answer to the same competition laws as everyone else, the Federal Trade Commission could police their rate agreements and mergers, courts would not have to defer to the federal Surface Transportation Board, and shippers could sue for triple damages when railroads violate antitrust law.
analysis.who_benefits: Shippers that move coal, grain, chemicals, and other freight by rail, and ultimately the households and businesses that pay prices carrying those freight costs. The bill requires the Surface Transportation Board to weigh the impact of rate agreements on shippers, consumers, and affected communities [S2] [S3], and lets customers injured by railroad antitrust violations collect treble damages without first filing a rate complaint [S2] [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail customers, and consumers paying freight costs

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the antitrust exemption for collective ratemaking agreements, so railroads can no longer set shipping rates together free of the Sherman and Clayton Acts [S2] [S3] [S4].
Allows injured parties to sue railroads for treble damages in antitrust cases, without regard to whether the railroad had filed rates or whether a rate complaint was pending [S2] [S3] [S4].

Puts FTC enforcement over rail rate agreements and lets the FTC weigh in on railroad mergers and acquisitions, and removes the requirement that courts defer to the Surface Transportation Board's primary jurisdiction in antitrust suits against railroads [S2] [S3] [S4].
Requires the Surface Transportation Board, when reviewing rate agreements and merger transactions, to take into account the impact on shippers, consumers, and affected communities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which would lose their century-old antitrust exemption and face antitrust suits, FTC regulation of rate agreements, and antitrust scrutiny of STB-approved mergers and acquisitions, with exposure to treble damages [S2] [S3] [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only going forward: no suit could be brought over conduct that occurred before enactment that was previously exempted, and new suits over previously exempt activity could not be filed until 180 days after enactment [S4].

Applying full antitrust litigation to rate agreements and mergers would add years of litigation and legal uncertainty for an industry the Surface Transportation Board already regulates, and shippers could ultimately bear some of that cost in rates; the bill also carves out an exception keeping pooled railcar arrangements exempt [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: railroads lose a legal shield that few industries enjoy, and their customers gain the ability to challenge anticompetitive rates, agreements, and mergers and recover damages. The strongest objection — that antitrust litigation layered on top of STB regulation adds cost and uncertainty — is real but modest next to what the exemption lets railroads do, since the bill keeps the STB in place and only removes the bar to competition-law review. The phase-in for past conduct limits disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee favorably and was placed on the Senate's calendar of business in December 2007, but the full Senate never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kohl introduced the bill on March 6, 2007 with ten original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1] [S4] [S6].

The Judiciary Committee held hearings in the Antitrust subcommittee in March and October 2007, and the Commerce Committee's surface transportation subcommittee held its own hearing in October 2007 [S6].

The Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on September 20, 2007, and it was reported with amendments by Senator Leahy on December 19, 2007, with written report No. 110-252 [S3] [S4] [S6].

The same day it was reported, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 551 — the list of bills awaiting floor action — where it sat without a floor vote through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S4] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major freight railroads, which kept their antitrust exemption for collective rate-setting and STB-approved mergers, and their largest customers on negotiated rates who faced no added competitive pressure. Shippers and consumers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — ten original cosponsors including two Republicans, and 11 total cosponsors split 9 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4] [S5] — but the Senate never voted, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: Railroads currently hold antitrust exemptions for collective rate agreements and STB-approved transactions, and are shielded from treble-damages suits [S2] [S3] [S4]. The bill would strip those shields, exposing rate-setting and mergers to antitrust review, FTC enforcement, and triple damages — the direct cost of the competition the bill restores.

industries.industry: Bulk freight shippers (grain, coal, chemicals, utilities)
industries.note: Shippers would gain the right to sue railroads for treble damages over anticompetitive conduct and to challenge collective rate agreements, and the STB would have to weigh effects on shippers and affected communities when reviewing agreements [S2] [S3]. Lower freight costs pass through to the prices consumers pay.
